accuracy.evidence: Every number checks out by hand. The 8 by 5 walk totals 26 cm. The missing sides are 30-26=4 cm for the pentagon, 26-20=6 cm for the quadrilateral and 30-25=5 cm for the regular hexagon. The rectangle pairs give 24 with 8 makes 4, 20 with 6 makes 4 and 30 with 10 makes 5. The 12-square shapes 12x1, 6x2 and 4x3 have perimeters 26, 16 and 14 cm.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors that the research on perimeter keeps finding: mixing up perimeter with area (counting squares inside), adding only the two labelled sides of a rectangle, subtracting a single 5 cm side instead of both equal sides, forgetting to halve, and assuming shapes with the same perimeter must enclose the same area or that the same area forces the same perimeter.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagperim lab is unlike the existing area and shape labs: an animated walker traces the edge while a running total builds, the child solves missing sides of a pentagon, triangle and regular shape, drags a corner to stretch a fixed 24 cm rectangle while its area readout changes, and rearranges twelve squares. It passed the shingle check against every other flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each rule is shown before it is stated. The child watches 8, 5, 8 and 5 add up to 26 as the walker goes round, discovers that a rectangle's sides come in equal pairs so perimeter minus two known sides then halved gives the other side, and sees the area peak at the 6 by 6 square while the perimeter stays at 24 cm.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions each have a tempting wrong option: the last side of a polygon when four sides already total 26 of 30 cm, the other side of a 24 cm rectangle with an 8 cm side (16 is the trap for subtracting once), and whether every rectangle with perimeter 24 cm has the same area. The child's guess is replayed after the task.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge rotates fresh questions and every wrong option has a tag with its own message: area for counting inside squares, two for adding only two sides, known and addp for subtraction slips, once and half for the rectangle steps, long and same for the area link, and count for miscounting a hexagon's six sides.

readability.evidence: The learner kid text scores about grade 3 and the adult text about grade 8.3 on Flesch-Kincaid, both inside the limits for the learner audience. Sentences are short, each lab step has one instruction, and terms like perimeter, polygon, regular and rectilinear are explained the first time they are used.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact, a method or a named mistake, with no warm-up sentences or repeated praise. The adult text names CCSS 3.MD.D.8 and the England Year 3 and Year 4 perimeter objectives, then lists the specific errors and how the lab tackles each one, with nothing restated across the paragraphs.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop in the browser gate. The corner drag uses A.gest so touch and mouse both work, the stretch caption moves below the rectangle on narrow screens so it no longer overlaps, and tap targets for the answer choices are large enough to hit with a thumb.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reported no violations in light or dark theme. The canvas has an aria-label, every drag action also has a button alternative, side lengths are labelled in text rather than by colour alone, and the lab colours come from A.col so contrast holds in both themes.
